practices.title: Establish requirements for success
practices.description:
Define performance, safety, and security benchmarks that establish the
baseline for existing and proposed systems to ensure AI-driven systems
align with the organization's mission and operational resilience goals
while achieving desired improvements. This ensures that the adoption of
AI delivers measurable operational value rather than purely
technological optimization.

These requirements provide a verifiable framework for system acceptance
and ongoing oversight, supporting clear accountability and
audit-readiness throughout the asset lifecycle.

This practice focuses on ensuring that the adoption of AI provides
measurable improvements. It is related to Practice 2: Define AI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service expectations, which ensures that
any trade-offs still result in acceptable overall levels of robustness,
resilience, and quality of service.

tasks.title: Identify current requirements
tasks.description:
Catalog the functional, safety, and performance requirements for the
operational processes the AI system is intended to support or augment.

This task ensures that AI-specific objectives are grounded in
established mission-critical benchmarks and provides the authoritative
framework for system acceptance and ongoing oversight. 

It also ensures that visibility is maintained into the expected
benefits to be gained relative to the trade-offs elsewhere, and
highlights when those benefits might no longer be present.

implementations.title: Operational baseline review
implementations.description:
Perform a baseline review of existing operational documentation, such
as safety manuals, standard operating procedures (SOPs), and service
level agreements (SLAs), for the targeted process. Distill these into a
"Requirements Summary" that explicitly lists measurable success
criteria (e.g., latency or throughput targets) along with minimum and
ideal thresholds for performance.

This implementation differs from Task 1.2: Create quantitative baselines for existing systems in both normal and challenging conditions by focusing on
establishing a baseline from which improvements can be measured.

proposed.text: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018, *Systems and software engineering — Life cycle processes — Requirements engineering*, which governs distilling existing documentation into a validated requirements and success-criteria summary, as this implementation describes.

implementations.title: Structured requirements mapping
implementations.description:
Conduct cross-functional requirements analysis with SMEs, including
those from engineering, safety, compliance, and legal departments, to
translate high-level mission goals into a structured requirements matrix
for the AI system. 

This matrix should map existing process requirements to specific AI
system constraints, defining both functional bounds (e.g., deterministic
setpoint (target value) limits, clinical dosage thresholds, or
transaction execution ceilings) and non-functional requirements (e.g.,
specific auditability standards and data retention periods).

proposed.text: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 (requirements traceability across stakeholders); NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 1 Rev. 1, *Engineering Trustworthy Secure Systems* (cited at Practice 2), whose requirements-traceability guidance applies to mapping mission goals to a structured requirements matrix.

tasks.title: Create quantitative baselines for existing systems in both normal and challenging conditions
tasks.description:
Establish quantitative performance baselines for current legacy or
manual processes to provide a comparative metric for evaluating AI
system effectiveness. 

These baselines capture performance under both normal and stressed
operating conditions, enabling technical managers to identify specific
risks and measure improvements associated with the adoption of AI.

This task differs from Implementation 1.1.1: Operational baseline review by focusing on
minimum performance under challenging conditions to ensure that
performance gains do not result in increased brittleness.

implementations.title: Establish manual or legacy process performance and safety baselines

proposed.text: "Document the current (pre-AI) performance and safety envelope of the manual or legacy process using existing operational records, historical incident logs, and subject-matter-expert interviews, capturing both steady-state performance and known failure modes. This baseline is the comparison point required by Task 1.2 and should be re-validated whenever the underlying process changes materially."
NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 1 Rev. 1; NIST SP 800-82r3 (cited at Practice 2 for OT baseline and impact characterization).

implementations.title: Develop high-fidelity operational baselines including edge-case performance under stress

proposed.text: "Extend the baseline from Implementation 1.2.1 with quantitative performance data captured under abnormal, degraded, or high-load conditions (for example, peak demand, component failure, adverse weather), drawn from historical incident data, simulation, or controlled stress testing where it is safe to do so. This is the baseline against which Task 2.3's TEVV protocols and Implementation 2.3.4's recurrent risk evaluations later measure performance drift."

tasks.title: Implement evaluation and test plans, including TEVV, across the AI lifecycle
tasks.description:
Develop and execute a systematic testing, evaluation, validation, and
verification (TEVV) program that assesses AI performance against
established requirements at each stage of the asset lifecycle, and
against previous baselines (if any). 

This task serves as the anchor for TEVV considerations throughout this
profile. It focuses on the generation of verifiable, audit-ready
evidence and ensures the system remains Valid and Reliable as physical
infrastructure or operational environments change. This task establishes
the baseline criteria for recurrent production-phase assessments
detailed in Implementation 2.3.4: Recurrent Risk Evaluations. 

Specialized applications of this framework appear throughout this
profile: Task 2.3: Establish protocols for and regularly perform systematic, and... extends TEVV to anomaly and edge-case behavior,
Implementation 4.1.3: Regularly practice and evaluate intervention processes applies TEVV
to override and intervention procedures, Implementation 7.5.2: Perform automated "champion-challenger"... applies
TEVV to champion-challenger drift assessment, and Task 11.4: Establish system integrity re-validation and re... applies TEVV to system
re-commissioning.

implementations.title: Define TEVV scope and requirements per AI system
implementations.description:
For AI systems deployed in safety-critical CI operational roles, define
TEVV scope requirements that are proportionate to consequence severity
of errors identified during risk assessments within Practice 3: Define risks, policies, and oversight for automated AI and agentic behavior and explicitly account for
CI-specific failure modes, including model drift, adversarial
manipulation, and degraded-mode operation. 

Establish pass/fail criteria for each lifecycle including
pre-deployment, post-incident, and periodic drift or degradation checks.
Test and Evaluation (T&E) planning documentation, of the kind already
used for many traditional CI systems to specify what will be tested,
under what conditions, and against what success criteria before testing
begins, provides a useful model for defining these requirements up
front, rather than determining them ad hoc during testing. Where an AI
system cannot be shown to satisfy reliability requirements for
autonomous operation, constrain it to a mode with increased human
oversight appropriate to the consequence severity of the application,
until TEVV evidence supports a higher level of autonomy. Ensure that
this temporary oversight mode does not exceed the documented cognitive
baseline of the available operators, as high algorithmic error rates
rapidly saturate human triage capacity. This may require use to be
limited to what can be supported by available human oversight capacity
as discussed in Task 4.4: Attention Governance and Alert/Alarm Flood Mitigation.

To prevent accidental operational outages caused by evaluation
overhead, procurement and engineering policies should explicitly
prohibit high-load active adversarial testing, automated input fuzzing,
or dense red-teaming (testing a system by deliberately seeking to
compromise it as an attacker would) vectors on live, production model
paths. All destructive profiling or exploratory boundary testing should
be restricted to isolated staging environments, offline
hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) test rigs, or high-fidelity digital twins
(detailed virtual replicas of physical equipment or processes that are
kept up to date with real data).

implementations.title: Categorization of Testing Environments
implementations.description:
TEVV activities across the system lifecycle should be conducted within
a validated environment tailored to the operational nature of the
underlying infrastructure:  

-   For critical applications where service delivery, safety
    constraints, or physical control loops cannot tolerate production
    path disruption or performance overhead, adhere to the production
    path testing prohibitions defined in Implementation 1.3.1: Define TEVV scope and requirements per AI.... Testing,
    including active verification, automated input fuzzing, and
    adversarial red-teaming should be restricted to non-production
    systems such as staging mirrors, hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) test
    rigs, simulators, or high-fidelity digital twins.
-   For critical applications that possess regular, planned downtime or
    can sustain temporary outages without safety impacts (e.g.,
    administrative or transactional batch processors, data summarization
    tools, or off-peak fraud queues), it may be safe to test directly on
    the active production system strictly during authorized maintenance
    or scheduled outage windows. Where feasible, this may be preferable
    to testing on simulators or staging systems, whose behavior may
    unintentionally differ from the live system.

tasks.title: Establish Domain Knowledge and Linguistic Alignment Requirements
tasks.description:
Identify and document the domain-specific knowledge, industry
terminology, and community context required for the AI system to perform
its intended function accurately and safely.

For pre-trained models or pre-built AI systems, establish success
criteria that mandate a verified understanding of sector-specific
jargon, operational nuances, and community variations to language,
particularly where colloquial variations exist.

This ensures that the system's outputs, whether in optimization,
predictive maintenance, digital twins, report summarization, or
AI-generated code, procedures, and configurations, are aligned with the
precise technical, conceptual, safety, and execution logic requirements
of the industry and the community it serves.

implementations.title: Maintenance & Operations
implementations.description:
For a predictive maintenance or digital twin system, require the AI to
demonstrate mastery of technical standards (e.g., distinguishing between
"forced outage" and "planned maintenance") to ensure correct
prioritization.

tasks.title: Establish AI usage thresholds and rate control mechanisms
tasks.description:
Define and implement technical constraints on the volume, frequency,
and scope of AI-driven actions, communications, and resource usage,
particularly where there are physical and safety limitations or
constrained resources.

This task reduces the potential for rapid, automated system instability
and resource bottlenecks by ensuring that AI interactions remain within
predefined operational tolerances and do not overwhelm upstream or
downstream legacy systems.

implementations.title: Implement baseline rate limiting
implementations.description:
Rate limit the various resources and actions that an AI system can
take, including consuming AI generation resources (often measured in
tokens), making configuration change requests, taking control actions,
and requesting attention from humans and other systems. 

This reduces the likelihood that automated activity will saturate
critical networks or cause instability in other systems, particularly
legacy systems that may not be designed for the rapid changes in
resource usage or control that can result from some AI systems. It may
also highlight signs of adversarial action or interference. 

Ensure that when rate limits are hit, the system's overall behavior
falls back to a safe state and that operators are notified via
non-disruptive alerts where appropriate (Tasks 3.4: Monitor for anomalous AI behavior and
4.2: Ensure that personnel are able to gain and maintain situational awareness).

This may be particularly important where AI is used to improve
efficiency in normal times, resulting in either more systems utilizing
the same allocated resources or the same systems being allocated fewer
resources. Such rate limits act as a first line of defense against
overload, particularly in unusual or unforeseen situations where the
efficiency gains may not hold. 

To safeguard operator cognitive capacity and minimize alert fatigue,
notification delivery metrics should follow the non-compulsory exception
batching, aggregation, and soft-throttling strategies outlined in Task
4.4: Attention Governance and Alert/Alarm Flood Mitigation.

cross_references.label: 3.4: Monitor for anomalous AI behavior
4.2: Ensure that personnel are able to gain and maintain situational awareness

implementations.title: Develop process-informed guardrails that dynamically determine the appropriate rate at which AI systems should be utilizing resources or taking actions. For example:
implementations.description:
-   An AI-based optimization system may use more tokens during quiet
    periods. 
-   Rapid changes to power grid load distribution should be avoided
    when the grid is running close to capacity. 

These guardrails should be deterministic and based on the
application's needs. Such guardrails give the AI system flexibility to
use additional resources or take additional actions when the application
requires it, such as during times of rapid change or heightened
activity, while maintaining tight control during quieter times.

implementations.title: Implement anomaly-driven detection and throttling based on patterns of expected behavior of the AI system, particularly in situations where tight guardrails may be difficult to develop.

tasks.title: Establish requirements for redundancy in AI-Driven functions
tasks.description:
Integrate independent, non-AI-based backup systems or parallel
processing paths for critical AI-dependent functions. 

This task directly preserves the system's Resilience by enforcing
graceful degradation to a known safe-state or manual control, reducing
the impact of a total loss of service due to AI component failure. This
task complements Task 3.4: Monitor for anomalous AI behavior.

cross_references.label: 3.4: Monitor for anomalous AI behavior

implementations.title: Maintain fully functional backup systems with documented, practiced fail-over procedures including the actions defined in Implementation [3.2.3: Specify fail-safe states and fallback behavior](#kix.fbdjwm7150p). Develop and communicate expected guarantees of performance during fail-over procedures so that downstream entities can prepare for potential impacts.

Deploy "watchdog" controllers based on independent, deterministic architectures that monitor AI output and automatically perform fail-over, consistent with Implementation [3.2.3: Specify fail-safe states and fallback behavior](#kix.fbdjwm7150p). Ensure the watchdog itself is included within Implementation [3.4.3: Monitor validation control integrity](#kix.h6w8xayde4wp). Notify operators of any watchdog-triggered fail-over per Task [4.2: Ensure that personnel are able to gain and maintain situational awareness](#kix.r74ert803tyq), so that a failure of the watchdog does not go undetected.

implementations.title: Baseline AI system performance
implementations.description:
Establish a "validated standard" dataset consisting of curated
historical inputs into the system for both normal and known-fault
conditions, and expected outputs, and expected levels of performance
against this dataset. This dataset should be regularly reviewed and
updated to account for drift in the environment, task, and/or expected
behavior. 

AI systems should be regularly tested against this dataset during
scheduled intervals as defined in Implementation 2.3.4: Recurrent Risk Evaluations and
deviations from acceptable thresholds for performance should be flagged
for review and remediation as necessary.

cross_references.label: 2.3.4: Recurrent Risk Evaluations

implementations.title: Targeted failure mode mapping
implementations.description:
Map the highest risk AI-specific behaviors in response to both
malicious attack (e.g., attacks listed in MITRE ATLAS and NIST AI
100-2e2025) as well as unintentional reasons (e.g., model drift).
Conduct regular adversarial testing of AI systems to verify system
behavior and proactively adjust or implement risk management controls
where appropriate.

implementations.title: Use Digital Twins to regularly test AI system behavior in response to anomalous conditions that are close to, or likely to result from, the system's current operational state.
Recurrent Risk Evaluations
implementations.description:
Establish a formalized, adaptive schedule to execute comprehensive
model risk evaluations of deployed systems. This is a scheduled,
batch-level evaluation; see Task 3.4: Monitor for anomalous AI behavior for continuous, runtime
anomaly detection and Implementation 3.3.2: Establish Maximum Drift Thresholds for the specific
drift thresholds that trigger fail-safe responses.

The baseline frequency of these evaluations should be dictated by an
explicit estimation of data/concept drift velocity and the volatility of
the application environment (e.g., seasonal process fluctuations, sensor
degradation curves, or shifting cyber threat landscapes).

Where feasible, determine a "Time-to-Divergence" baseline during
pre-deployment staging - estimating how quickly the model's accuracy
degrades under simulated environmental shifts. Where historical incident
or drift data is too limited to support a confident quantitative
estimate, organizations should use the best available approximation
(e.g., expert judgment or analogous systems) and revise the cadence as
real operational data accumulates, rather than treating the initial
estimate as fixed. 

The evaluation cadence should be set to a fraction of this estimated
divergence time (e.g., if a model historically begins to drift
significantly over 90 days due to seasonal variations, organizations are
encouraged to set the evaluation and recalibration cadence to sub-90-day
intervals). Out-of-cycle evaluations should be triggered automatically
if continuous telemetry indicates that actual drift velocity is
accelerating faster than the estimated baseline.

To execute these evaluations without impacting availability or safety,
organizations should follow Implementation 1.3.2: Categorization of Testing Environments. 

Systems should be tested against the "validated standard" datasets
maintained under Implementation 2.3.1: Baseline AI system performance to quantify statistical
drift, concept drift, and shifts in error distributions (such as false

1.2: Create quantitative baselines for existing systems in both normal and challenging conditions or intersect with the boundaries defined in Implementation

system should initiate formal change-management or mitigation workflows.
These workflows may include model retraining, throttling via Task
2.1: Establish AI usage thresholds and rate control mechanisms, or transitioning the
process to the backup as specified in Implementation [2.2.1: Maintain fully functional backup systems ]{.c12

tasks.title: Perform Linguistic and Domain-Context Robustness Testing
tasks.description:
Integrate domain-specific linguistic and contextual validation into the
system's TEVV protocols. This practice ensures that the AI
system---especially when utilizing pre-trained models---remains robust
and reliable when encountering specialized industry terminology,
operational jargon, or community-specific language. The goal is to
prevent failure modes where linguistic ambiguity or a lack of domain
awareness leads to incorrect system actions, safety-critical
"hallucinations," or the misprioritization of critical infrastructure
alerts.

implementations.title: Benchmarking on application-specific terminology
implementations.description:
Develop or utilize sector-specific datasets that include significant
application-specific terminology. This includes ambiguous operational
terms (e.g., distinguishing between a "soft trip" and a "hard
shutdown"), colloquial terms used by different roles in the sector, and
terms whose application- and role-specific meanings differ from
conventional use. This dataset should be used to measure the model's
precision in interpreting application-specific text, such as in
summarizing reports, interpreting natural language instructions, and
performing internal and external-facing chatbot tasks.

implementations.title: Localization and Community Validation
implementations.description:
For customer-facing or public-sector systems, test the AI's robustness
against regional dialects and community-specific terminology to ensure
equitable and accurate delivery of information across the service
area.

implementations.title: Technical Accuracy and "Plausible Hallucination" Audits
implementations.description:
Implement specific TEVV protocols to identify "plausible-sounding but
technically inaccurate" outputs. 

For AI systems providing or generating diagnostics, maintenance
summaries, operational advice, procedures, code, or configurations, use
subject matter experts to at least spot-check and/or assist in
red-teaming the system's instructions. This testing should focus on
edge cases where the AI might generate incorrect maintenance steps that
appear valid on the surface but would damage physical assets or violate
safety protocols if executed.

tasks.title: Verify and Ensure Policy Robustness Against Component, Hardware, and Data Schema Variance
tasks.description:
Ensure that learning systems that optimize their behavior, such as
reinforcement learning systems, do not learn to rely on undocumented or
out-of-specification behavior of their target system. 

Such dependence may cause suboptimal system behavior, failure, or
damage if the AI system is subsequently deployed on, or interacts with,
other systems that have identical specifications but behave differently
outside of their specified parameters. 

For example, an AI system to optimize pressure levels in an industrial
system might be trained on a system that happens to have a valve that
happens to be able to open wider than required by the system's
specifications, which might only set a minimum flow rate. If this AI
system is subsequently deployed to control a different system with the
same specifications, but where the valve just meets specifications, the
system may behave in an undesirable manner. 

This task also supports Implementation 7.5.4: Audit Interoperability for Hardware or Data Substrate Substitution .

implementations.title: Train Across the Full Operating Range
implementations.description:
AI systems that are trained in a very narrow part of the operating
range can become dependent on parameters remaining within the range
observed in training, even if operational conditions can legitimately
deviate from this. 

To counter this, when training optimization models, particularly
via simulations or digital twins, intentionally randomize and cycle
environmental parameters to the absolute limits allowed (e.g., maximum
and minimum rated latencies, tolerances, thermal thresholds, new vs worn
equipment and sensors, different weather conditions, etc.). 

When training on physical hardware, ensure that training and testing is
performed on a representative set of functionally equivalent equipment
that the system is likely to encounter in deployment, including
equipment at different levels of wear and subject to different
environmental conditions. 

For AI systems that can take symbolic background knowledge, ensure that
the formal specifications of component systems are appropriately encoded
into the AI system so that the learning process avoids relying on
capabilities outside of those specifications. 

This prevents the AI from building a policy that breaks when, for
instance, a component operates at a different but legally compliant
point within its spec sheet.

implementations.title: Multi-Vendor Testing
implementations.description:
For high-consequence systems, mandate that the AI system's validation
includes testing in simulation environments, digital twins, and/or
dedicated test-rigs. These should include equivalent parts from
different manufacturers and at different levels of wear and tear that
are representative of what may appear in the environments that the AI
system would be deployed in over time. This is necessary to detect
hidden, non-generalized model behavioral strategies (learned policies),
such as a hidden reliance on capabilities that may be outside of the
physical parts' specifications. 

For time-critical systems, testing should be performed on
non-production environments as specified in Implementation
1.3.2: Categorization of Testing Environments.

tradespace of the risks and benefits of using the AI system, and the
costs associated with controls that may be needed.

implementations.title: Identify AI system decision points and potential outcomes of AI system errors
implementations.description:
Determine decision points that may be affected by errors in
AI-generated outputs (e.g. control action, predictions, recommendations,
summaries, code, procedures, or system configurations) and how they can
influence operations, including downstream effects. 

In addition to unintentional errors, consider decision points where a
capable adversary could deliberately manipulate AI-generated outputs to
achieve a specific harmful outcome, distinct from the AI simply
malfunctioning on its own.

Examples of errors include false positives/negatives, increased
measurement bias, reduced precision, incorrect interpretation of
instructions, or increased delay in output. 

Examples of downstream effects include: 

-   An AI-based machine vision system for detecting the presence and
    extent of defects can affect the actions of both automated systems
    as well as humans, such as if they over- or under-estimate defects.
    
-   Conventional productivity tools, such as report summarizers,
    applied to summarizing technical condition reports, affect the
    decisions made by humans who rely on the summaries, particularly if
    they fail to recognize application-specific terminology
    (Implementation 2.4.1: Benchmarking on application-specific terminology) and erroneously
    omit mentions of signs of imminent failure.

implementations.title: Define acceptable risk thresholds and associated control responses
implementations.description:
Establish threshold criteria that bound acceptable AI behavior in terms
of impact severity, likelihood, and recovery feasibility. Consider NIST
SP 800-30 r1 sections 3.1 to 3.3 and Appendices G,H, and I to implement
risk assessments for each of the decision points. 

When establishing risk thresholds, avoid over-indexing on purely
technical, point-in-time metrics, whether traditional vulnerability
scoring systems (such as the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS))
or raw algorithmic performance benchmarks (such as model confidence
scores, error rates, or statistical accuracy). Instead, utilize
consequence-driven frameworks, drawing on the operational prioritization
logic of models like Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization
(SSVC), to evaluate risks based on real-world impacts to public health,
safety, and mission continuity.

Associate these risk thresholds with a defined organizational response
such as enforced action, system isolation, authority throttling, or
operator escalation.

Review these risk thresholds and control responses as the AI system,
task, and operational environment change.

tasks.title: Implement independent guardrails ("safety wrappers") for AI outputs
tasks.description:
Enclose AI systems within hard-coded, deterministic guardrails (or
boundary logic) that do not depend on AI and detect if safety
constraints are likely to be violated and take appropriate actions to
maintain functional safety. 

Such actions may include limiting the AI system's output, engaging
fallback controllers and plans, notifying human operators, and logging.

Independent, deterministic safety wrappers add a critical layer of
defense alongside emergency software patching cycles during active
exploits. By enforcing hard-coded constraints at the operational
boundary, these wrappers ensure that even if an upstream AI system is
completely compromised at machine speed, unsafe commands or invalid data
transactions are structurally blocked.

Align these measures with Practice 4: Define procedures for emergency avoidance override, recovery, and situation awareness and in particular Task
4.4: Attention Governance and Alert/Alarm Flood Mitigation to integrate
appropriate, timely, and feasible human intervention, and with Practice
10: Implement multi-tiered AI system logging and audit capabilities to ensure visibility
into the AI system's attempted behavior, even when guardrails prevent
actual harm.

implementations.title: Define deterministic, operational constraints that the AI system should remain within
implementations.description:
Define the boundary that the AI system should remain within for safe
operation. These might be in- and out-of-range values, semantic and
behavioral constraints, rate-of-change violations, and deterministic
logical constraints that should be respected regardless of the AI
system's confidence level. 

These deterministic constraints should be defined and enforced
independent of the AI system's internal logic (e.g., at the physical
process boundary). These constraints should reflect the most restrictive
combination of the organization's, equipment's, application's, and the
AI system's safe operating limits (including the limits of the AI
system's training).

Constraints should apply uniformly to all automated command sources at
the physical process boundary, including AI recommendations, automated
agents, remote operator sessions, and any other upstream system.
Authentication and physical safety are separate concerns: confirming who
or what sent a command (addressed in Practice 5: Implement identity and access management (IdAM) for AI agents...) does not guarantee that
the command itself is safe to execute. An authenticated source can still
issue a damaging command through error, misconfiguration, or compromise.
Absent an explicit, authorized override, such safety wrappers should
intercept physically unsafe commands regardless of their source. 

Where such constraints must be lifted, e.g., to facilitate an
experienced human engineer remotely dealing with a novel situation, such
constraints should be explicitly overridden in accordance with emergency
safety protocols.
The same principle of independently-enforced constraints applies beyond
physical process control: for AI systems that generate or filter
information rather than direct commands, the "constraint" may be one
of required completeness or fidelity, independently enforced regardless
of the AI system's own judgment about what is relevant.

For example:

-   An attacker gaining access to a plant human-machine interface (HMI)
    could issue setpoint commands indistinguishable from legitimate AI
    recommendations. 
-   A valve controlled by an AI system might have constraints that the
    AI system may not have properly learned, such as not being opened
    and closed in quick succession, and not being opened at the same
    time as another valve. 
-   A condition report summarization tool should be constrained to
    include information about every asset, even if the AI system judges
    a given condition not to be of concern.
-   An AI system routing high-volume transactions or processing patient
    records should be bounded by deterministic validation rules that
    block anomalous account or resource allocations (e.g., assigning an
    atomic resource to two entities), prevent unauthorized data
    aggregation, or flag out-of-bounds risk parameters prior to
    downstream operational execution.

implementations.title: Specify fail-safe states and fallback behavior
implementations.description:
Define deterministic states the control system should enter when AI
output violates the constraints defined in 3.2.2: Define deterministic, operational constraints that the AI system should remain within, or when the AI system
becomes unavailable or degraded. 

These fail-safe states should incorporate clear protocols for tracking
algorithmic state consistency during failover and re-commissioning
cycles. Recovery logic should explicitly dictate whether an overridden
AI agent resumes operations by synchronizing with its last active
context window, resetting to a validated baseline template state, or
gracefully de-escalating control to a legacy deterministic controller,
preventing sudden uncommanded physical actions from an un-synchronized
model state.

For example:

-   If an AI system commands a valve to be opened while another
    incompatible valve is also open, the system might fall back onto a
    less optimal, but known-safe non-AI controller to determine, for the
    current plant state, which valve has precedence. 
-   If a device loses communication with its AI-based controller, it
    might default to a pre-defined safe state and broadcast an alert,
    rather than executing a possibly corrupted last AI-issued
    command.

This task should be aligned with those of Practice 4: Define procedures for emergency avoidance override, recovery, and situation awareness so that immediate-term
automated fail-safe and fallback policies are visible to, and align
with, subsequent human intervention.

implementations.title: Define further logging and communication actions
implementations.description:
Specify logging and communication actions that the organization should
take when AI outputs violate constraints. Actions can include notifying
necessary operators and systems, and enabling enhanced logging to
provide further details. 

For example, when a validation control rejects an AI-generated shutdown
command on a generation unit, the plant control room, operators and any
connected systems should be notified, and the incident logged along with
associated information that may be necessary to update the AI
system.

Alarms tracking such failures should be throttled or rate-limited
rather than flooding operator consoles and logs with repetitive
rejection events. For example, multiple identical failures could be
consolidated into a single notification. See Task 4.4: Attention Governance and Alert/Alarm Flood Mitigation for further
details.

tasks.title: Establish Failure Notification Requirements
tasks.description:
Define the operational conditions under which an AI system should
overtly assert a state of exception ("fail loudly") versus when it may
attempt autonomous error recovery, clearly distinguishing notification
alerts from physical fail-safe states. This task ensures that for
high-consequence applications, operators maintain sufficient situational
awareness to make timely, informed intervention decisions and are
protected against undetected operational drift caused by "quiet" AI
failures.

This is particularly important in multi-system and agentic workflows,
where failures in one agent may be unintentionally masked by the
resilience of other agents, silently reducing safety margins, degrading
performance, or causing preventable damage. 

The need to "fail loudly" should be considered carefully against the
limited attention span of human (or AI) supervisors to avoid "alarm
flood" situations, where a large number of "high priority" alarms reduce
the ability to address the underlying problem, especially when unusual
failures happen as discussed in Task 4.4: Attention Governance and Alert/Alarm Flood Mitigation.

implementations.title: Context-Specific Failure Modes
implementations.description:
Conduct an engineering assessment for each application to determine its
failure notification requirements. 

For example, silent resilience (e.g., automated retries or soft
failovers) may be appropriate for non-critical administrative tasks
where internal algorithmic recovery does not alter physical processes or
mask safety margins. 

Conversely, for safety-critical IT/OT/ICS applications, a 'fail
loudly' protocol should be enforced with explicit human notifications,
even if the system continues to operate, perhaps in a degraded capacity.

These notification states should be programmatically linked to the
independent safety wrappers in Task 3.2: Implement independent guardrails ("safety wrappers") for AI... to ensure that an unacknowledged 'loud' failure automatically
forces a transition to a deterministic fallback state (per
Implementation 3.2.3: Specify fail-safe states and fallback...).

To prevent alarm floods and alert fatigue, utilize containment
techniques such as time-delay hysteresis, dynamic deadbands (control and
sensor ranges where minor fluctuations are ignored and assumed to be
noise), and state-based alarm aggregation to compress rapid automated
iterations into a single operational event change. See Task
4.4: Attention Governance and Alert/Alarm Flood Mitigation for further details.

implementations.title: Establish Maximum Drift Thresholds
implementations.description:
Establish quantitative monitoring and thresholds against which the AI
system is continuously or periodically evaluated for how far the
real-world operating environment, data inputs, task, and system context
can shift from the historic conditions on which the system was trained
before mitigations are put in place, defining the specific thresholds
that determine when the periodic evaluations in Implementation
2.3.4: Recurrent Risk Evaluations or the continuous monitoring in Task 3.4: Monitor for anomalous AI behavior should
trigger a fail-safe response. 

Determine if such a "distribution fuse" or "distribution circuit
breaker" should include notifications, forced fail-over, or other
restrictions on the operation of the system. 

Minimum responses should include operator notification. For
safety-critical applications, responses should include automatic
restriction of AI authority or forced failover to a deterministic backup
system. 

Drift thresholds should account for seasonal, operational, and
environmental variation relevant to the CI sector, in addition to the
physical degradation and changes over time of underlying OT hardware.

For example, an AI model trained on summer demand patterns in a water
distribution system should have explicit thresholds that detect and flag
degraded performance during winter conditions before that degradation
can cause operators to miss a safety-relevant alert. Similarly, a
healthcare diagnostic AI should flag clinical drift when shifted between
different patient demographics, and a financial liquidity model should
trigger boundaries during sudden, non-historical macroeconomic
shocks.

Drift thresholds should be reviewed and recalibrated at a defined
interval or whenever a significant change in the operational environment
occurs.

This implementation mitigates hazard risk associated with silent AI
performance degradation. An AI model trained on historical operational
data progressively loses accuracy as the operational environment shifts,
without generating any visible failure or alert. Operators could
continue to rely on the AI's outputs without realizing its reliability
has degraded below acceptable thresholds.

tasks.title: Define and control risks to adjacent and related systems
tasks.description:
Define and control risks to other systems that may be affected by a
failure in this system, including: 

-   Systems that are intentionally interdependent with this system,
    where errors travel along functional, data, or operational
    dependencies ("cascading failures").
-   Systems that may be unrelated except for shared adjacency in a
    physical, logical, network, resource, supply chain, or other sense
    ("splash damage" or "blast radius").

implementations.title: Map direct functional and algorithmic dependencies
implementations.description:
Trace and document downstream logical, algorithmic, and operational
paths of AI outputs to identify how errors, whether in control outputs,
direct executable code, or human-mediated summaries, could trigger a
chain reaction through connected assets. 

These dependencies often extend beyond traditional IT/OT/ICS
boundaries; for example, an AI agent defending an IT network might
erroneously disable authentication traffic, physically locking personnel
out of a facility. 

To fully capture these risks, organizations should conduct a high-value
asset (HVA) assessment that extends outward to map functional
dependencies on upstream suppliers and downstream customers, ensuring
automated errors do not propagate along the extended supply chain.

implementations.title: Identify indirect shared infrastructure and collateral damage exposure
implementations.description:
Audit the operational environment to identify functionally independent
systems that are vulnerable to collateral damage from an AI failure.
Evaluation criteria should include cross-cutting environmental and
infrastructure commonalities, such as:

-   Physical Proximity: Independent physical assets co-located in the
    same facility or enclosure, or that share the same power, cooling,
    or other physical resources.
-   Network Topography: Systems sharing the same network switches,
    backbones, or uplink paths.
-   Logical Substrates: Unrelated applications sharing the same
    hypervisor, underlying cloud tenant, base operating system image, or
    database instance.

This mapping should also consider whether a single event or action
could affect multiple identified safeguards at once, rather than
assuming redundant controls fail independently.

This asset assessment should, where possible, reach outward past the
facility's immediate perimeter to evaluate shared municipal substrates,
such as the regional electrical grid, water networks, or
telecommunication backbones, where a localized AI failure or
resource-saturation event could cause regional collateral damage. 

Where direct technical visibility or telemetry past the facility's
perimeter is unavailable, organizations should utilize qualified
engineering approximations and best-available sector intelligence to
estimate these external impacts. These estimations must be explicitly
documented as bounded technical assumptions to ensure transparency
regarding data limitations, preventing the assessment from stalling due
to incomplete external information.

The task of mapping internal dependencies is common to Implementation
7.6.1: Internal Dependency Mapping (Orphan System Prevention). Maintaining this map
can reduce the effort needed when this system is later
decommissioned.

cross_references.label: 7.6.1: Internal Dependency Mapping (Orphan System Prevention)

implementations.title: Impact compartmentalization (sandboxing)
implementations.description:
Restrict AI agent execution to isolated micro-segments of the network
or other infrastructure. For example, an AI optimizing valve pressure
should not be able to affect core safety instrumented systems (SIS).

implementations.title: Define and implement resource limiting
implementations.description:
Identify limited resources that the AI agent or system shares with
other systems (AI or otherwise), such as compute, tokens, exclusive
hardware/sensor access, power, network bandwidth, and cooling. Define
and implement appropriate soft and hard limits on the AI system's use of
these resources, along with appropriate notifications for when these
limits are approached or exceeded.

tasks.title: Mitigate automation complacency and skills degradation
tasks.description:
Establish continuous readiness and training protocols to counter
creeping dependence on AI systems. This task requires organizations to
identify critical human capabilities that should be preserved, ensuring
that operators retain the technical expertise, cognitive situational
awareness, and manual override proficiency necessary to manage
operations during prolonged AI outages or catastrophic failures.

implementations.title: Baseline Human Competency Retention
implementations.description:
Identify and document the core operational skills (e.g., manual loop
tuning, raw data interpretation, manual dispatch) that risk being eroded
by day-to-day AI reliance. 

Incorporate periodic, audited training or, commensurate with available
operational resources, simulator-based testing to verify that human
operators can safely run the infrastructure without AI assistance.

implementations.title: Scheduled "Manual Control" Drills
implementations.description:
Where appropriate, establish a routine cadence of scheduled operational
drills analogous to facility "live-load generator exercising" or
"blackout drills" in OT, paper-based charting and manual triage cycles
in healthcare, or offline transaction reconciliation procedures in
finance. During designated low-risk or off-peak windows, simulate a
failure of the AI system. The failure could include a loss of
availability or a combination of other failures as identified in
3.1: Identify risk tradeoffs.

These drills should be designed to achieve two primary outcomes:

-   Technical Validation: Verify that fallback deterministic control
    systems, analog backups, and safety interlocks successfully assume
    the operational load without data loss or safety breaches.
-   Human Readiness: Force human operators to actively manage
    operations via legacy or manual methods, preserving the critical
    muscle memory, tactical domain skills, and situational awareness
    required to safely navigate a real-world, unannounced AI
    outage.

For applications where this is not possible within safety or regulatory
constraints, they should be performed within non-production systems, see
Implementation 1.3.2: Categorization of Testing Environments for further details.

implementations.title: Cognitive Engagement Monitoring
implementations.description:
Design the human-machine interface (HMI) to prevent passive monitoring.
Consider active human verification step-throughs or "sanity checks"
for truly high-consequence AI recommendations to counter the
psychological tendency of operators to automatically trust machine
outputs (automation bias).

To manage the critical tradespace between active human validation and
cognitive exhaustion, these checkpoints should be reserved strictly for
high-consequence operational boundary thresholds. They should be
deployed flexibly, utilizing the mixed-initiative and calm technology
design choices referenced in Task 4.4: Attention Governance and Alert/Alarm Flood Mitigation to
prevent alert fatigue from driving superficial operator
compliance.

Establish organizational policies, procurement gates, and contractor
onboarding workflows to detect, restrict, and manage risks associated
with unvetted or unauthorized AI systems, localized open-source
foundational models, and agentic tools brought into the operational
environment by internal personnel or third-party contractors. This task
ensures that any AI capability utilized within the facility's physical
or logical boundary is explicitly accounted for in the organization's
risk profile and configuration management baselines.

tasks.description:
Define procedures by which authorized, trained personnel can safely
override AI-driven actions in a timely manner during an emergency

override access control in the event of a fire or other emergency.

Note that in many applications, simply disabling the AI system can
leave the overall system in an unsafe state. This task should establish
overall procedures for personnel to obtain appropriate situational
awareness (Task 4.2: Ensure that personnel are able to gain and maintain situational awareness),
and decide on the appropriate action to take. These should align with

implementations.title: Ensure that AI systems can be reliably overridden
implementations.description:
Ensure that technical processes for intervening in the AI system's
operation are reliably implemented at appropriate points. For example,

termination policies that can also be followed for containerized AI

implementations.title: Establish tiered intervention procedures, training, and authorization
implementations.description:
Implement or utilize existing tiered training, authorization, and
access control for personnel intervening in AI system operation. This
may include requiring multiple personnel to be available to authorize
particularly high impact interventions. 

Examples of tiers could include placing the system into "emergency
mode," overriding individual actions, partial suspension of operation,
and full system isolation. 

Ensure that sufficient appropriately trained and authorized personnel
are available commensurate with the system's designated autonomy level
and operational criticality, or where real-time human intervention is
explicitly required as an active risk mitigation control. 

Consider an "emergency mode" protocol for external emergency response
personnel who may need to safely isolate or override the AI system in an
emergency situation. This may be important for reasons that include:

-   Organizational personnel may be unable to safely approach or
    communicate with the AI system during an emergency. 
-   AI systems may behave in ways that responding personnel may not
    expect and who may not have time or resources to address. 
-   Emergencies and other incidents may generate inputs into the AI
    system that it does not expect and for which it may not have been
    tested, resulting in greater probability of erroneous and
    inappropriate outputs. 

For example, during a fire or chemical emergency, or in a widespread
disaster situation, organizational personnel may be unable to safely
approach or communicate with a remote facility. Responders may need
out-of-band emergency interfaces, like secured external emergency stop
buttons (E-stops) (subject to applicable functional-safety certification
requirements, such as IEC 60204-1, independent of any AI-specific
considerations), to place AI-enabled systems into a known safe
state.

For high-consequence systems, consider whether decision-making
authority should be pre-established for scenarios where the underlying
cause of an anomaly isn't yet clear, so that responders aren't delayed
during a machine-speed event, adversarial or otherwise.

tasks.title: Ensure that personnel are able to gain and maintain situational awareness
tasks.description:
Implement role-appropriate mechanisms for providing personnel with
rapid, actionable situational awareness as to the state of the AI
system, its task, recent decisions, environment, and anomalies. 

The goal is to reduce the likelihood of humans making mistakes when
overriding the AI system, particularly in chaotic, emergency, unusual,
time-sensitive, and high pressure situations. 

This may take the form of displays, interfaces to existing information
management tools, printouts, or a combination that aims to reduce the
cognitive latency required for an operator to transition from passive
monitoring to active intervention. Risk management should account for
the operational latency required to comprehend a machine-speed cascade
from a cold start.

Care should be taken to ensure that the mechanisms do not cause
cognitive overload or confusion, particularly for those who may be
unfamiliar with the system, such as external responders and maintenance
personnel. See Task 4.4: Attention Governance and Alert/Alarm Flood Mitigation for additional
considerations.

implementations.title: Develop situational awareness processes and procedures for personnel who may need to intervene in the AI system's operation
implementations.description:
Divide personnel into groups based on the decisions that they will be
expected to make in intervening in the AI system (including assessing
the need to intervene), and their expected background knowledge. 

Include personnel who regularly work with the system as well as those
who may need to interact with the system at short notice, during an
incident, and in an emergency. 

For example:

-   Engineers who work with the system day-to-day may require a summary
    of deviations from normal operation to anticipate and avoid
    potential incidents. These summaries avoid important information
    from being buried within "normal" status reports that they may
    become accustomed to skimming over. 
-   External maintenance engineers, who may be familiar with the
    equipment family but not the specific installation, may benefit from
    a combination of printed material and dynamic displays that
    highlight how this AI system's operational learning has caused its
    behavior to differ from a generic or freshly deployed system,
    allowing them to avoid taking actions that would ordinarily be safe
    but may pose a risk for this specific deployment. 
-   Emergency responders who may be non-technical and need to make
    decisions under time pressure may only need just enough information
    to decide which of a pre-set number of emergency modes to put the
    system in, such as reverting to a "safe" controller or shutting down
    the system completely.

implementations.title: Regularly evaluate situational awareness mechanisms
implementations.description:
Test situational awareness mechanisms on a regular basis, to both
ensure that they appropriately reflect the underlying state of the AI
system, and that their intended audience appropriately understands them.
This should be combined with Implementation 4.1.3: Regularly practice and evaluate intervention processes.

in the AI system's operation have access to the necessary information
independent of the AI system's functionality. 

Akin to the analog gauges present on aircraft that otherwise have fully
digital cockpits, these mechanisms allow for situational awareness,
control, and risk management even when a fault renders AI-mediated
channels untrustworthy or unavailable.

tasks.title: Attention Governance and Alert/Alarm Flood Mitigation
tasks.description:
Treat human attention as a finite resource that AI systems should use
efficiently. AI-driven notification volume can exceed an operator's
ability to triage, reducing effectiveness rather than improving it. This
may be by overwhelming a domain with no prior experience managing this
risk, breaking the assumptions behind a domain's existing alarm flood
mitigations, or generating a correlated surge across many systems at
once. 

This task complements Task 4.2: Ensure that personnel are able to gain and maintain... by
addressing cases where notification volume, not just notification
content or clarity, is what threatens an operator's ability to respond
effectively.

implementations.title: Recognizing novel AI-driven alert floods in unfamiliar domains
implementations.description:
Domains with no prior experience managing alarm floods may not
recognize the pattern when AI introduces it, or know that established
mitigation techniques exist. For example, a fraud-detection system
entering a confused state can flood a review queue with false positives;
a summarization tool can generate excessive content when it should stay
silent; a hospital's AI-assisted clinical decision support can generate
alert volumes comparable to those long documented in traditional medical
device alarm fatigue, but without the institutional awareness built up
around that older problem.

Measures to reduce this risk range from training personnel to recognize
alert-flood patterns as they emerge in the tool they're using and
developing procedures for manual prioritization, to automated triage and
consolidation of output (e.g., rate-limiting generated content, grouping
duplicate flags).

implementations.title: Adapting legacy alarm management for AI's non-deterministic failure modes
implementations.description:
Domains with mature, trusted alarm-management practices may find those
practices don't transfer cleanly to some AI systems. Traditional
mitigations often assume alarms correspond to discrete, mechanical fault
states (e.g., a stuck valve or tripped breaker). 

Examples of ways in which AI-generated alarms can differ from those in
more traditional systems include: 

-   An AI system may report the same underlying error in slightly
    different ways. 
-   Adaptive AI systems may respond inconsistently to an underlying
    error, resulting in hidden or inconsistent alarms.
-   Inconsistent AI alerts may result in only downstream systems
    alerting while the system that is the root cause stays silent.
    
-   Agentic systems build dependencies dynamically and in an
    undocumented manner, so a failure may cause unexpected and seemingly
    unrelated systems to send notifications of failure. 
-   Machine learned detection algorithms and thresholds may be
    undocumented and applied inconsistently, making it difficult to
    determine what any given alert means. 

The dependency mapping in Implementations 3.5.1: Map direct functional and algorithmic dependencies and 3.5.2: Identify indirect shared infrastructure and collateral damage exposure can help
make these dependency chains more visible in advance, even though it
does not resolve the underlying detection problem.

Some partial, non-CI-specific and non-AI-specific approaches exist in
the broader IT/software observability field, such as similarity-based
alert clustering and distributed tracing, but these generally assume
mature instrumentation that most current AI deployments, and especially
OT environments, do not yet have in place. This is particularly
challenging in agentic systems, which make dependency decisions in a
dynamic and undocumented fashion.

implementations.title: Managing correlated multi-system attention surges
implementations.description:
A single external event can trigger a simultaneous surge of attention
requests across many AI-controlled systems at once, overwhelming a
limited pool of human operators even if each individual system's alert
volume is otherwise manageable. In cases where the adoption of AI has
coincided with a reduction in staffing levels, this can result in a lack
of on-call or appropriately trained operators to address sudden issues.

For example, a widespread power failure or loss of traffic signals can
cause an entire autonomous vehicle fleet to simultaneously request
remote operator attention, exceeding the capacity of the remote
operations center.

Measures to address this risk include:

-   Identifying which AI-driven systems share a human supervision pool,
    and estimating what external events could cause them to request
    attention simultaneously. 
-   Design and resource supervision capacity and escalation procedures
    explicitly for correlated worst-case surges, not just average or
    independent per-system load.
-   Developing automated alert triaging mechanisms so that limited
    operator attention is not spent sorting through large quantities of
    alerts or addressing low priority issues.

implementations.title: Applying consolidation and low-cognitive-load design techniques
implementations.description:
Once alarm flood risks are identified, apply techniques that reduce the
rate and cognitive cost of notifications without hiding genuinely
urgent, isolated signals. 

Examples of measures to consider include: 

-   Implementing basic consolidation, such as grouping repeated
    identical alerts into a single notification.
-   Applying user-interface design choices that reduce distraction
    (often referred to as calm-technology or mixed-initiative
    interfaces) such as exception batching, trend dashboards, dynamic
    deadbands, time-delay hysteresis, matched to the specific
    application, supervision model, and the range of personnel
    familiarity likely to encounter these notifications, from regular
    operators to occasional external responders.

Note that there is a trade-off between many of these measures. For
example, aggressive batching reduces fatigue but risks delaying a
genuinely urgent, isolated signal.

tasks.title: Define operational regimes for human-on-the-loop and human-out-of-the-loop operation
tasks.description:
Identify operational contexts where real-time, manual human-in-the-loop
(HITL) oversight is physically or technically infeasible due to tight
system time constants (such as stability anomalies operating in
milliseconds, real-time industrial control loops, or machine-speed cyber
defense events). Human oversight degrades into a purely nominal or
superficial check if the required cognitive review and validation
latency exceeds the system's physical action time, particularly in
situations where fatigue or stress are factors. 

For these regimes, formally define the boundaries where
human-on-the-loop (supervisory oversight with delayed intervention
capability) or human-out-of-the-loop (autonomous execution with
retrospective post-hoc review) should substitute for active human
control, and specify the deterministic automated protections required to
support them.

This task prevents dangerous operational dependencies on human reaction
times during rapid, cascading physical anomalies. It ensures that when
humans cannot act as an immediate safety-net, automated boundaries step
in to preserve system stability.

practices.title: Implement identity and access management (IdAM) for AI agents, systems, and tools
practices.description:
Establish IdAM controls for AI agents and tools appropriate to their
roles, auditability, risk, and oversight, at points in the AI system
lifecycle from deployment through to decommissioning. 

Establishing these boundaries reduces the risk of malicious or
unauthorized actions reaching risk-sensitive processes, and limits the
impacts across the operational environment. 

Controls modelled after human user permissions are a starting point but
access should be further restricted based on actual need of individual
AI agents and tools.

tasks.title: Require identities and authentication for AI entities
tasks.description:
Inventory AI entities and define authentication requirements that
uniquely identify each AI entity, including those that are ephemeral,
and ensure those identities are distinct across system boundaries,
operational roles, and multi-agent deployment.

In this task, an AI entity refers to an invocation of an AI agent or
tool that performs atomic tasks, at a suitable level of granularity, and
whose behavior should be meaningfully traced and disambiguated from the
behavior of other invocations of the same or similar AI agents and
tools. If the AI entity is compromised or otherwise found to be behaving
in an undesired manner, the level of granularity should be sufficient to
identify and revoke access while minimizing the effect on other AI
entities. 

The appropriate level of granularity will vary depending on variables
that include: 

-   Available resources (finance, time, expertise). 
-   Expected threat level. 
-   Expected impact. 
-   Other mitigating controls. 
-   Scale. 
-   Vendor co-operation. 
-   Application complexity. 

Organizations should implement this task flexibly, to allow for changes
in granularity as these variables change. 

Where this is not possible, such as with legacy or compute-constrained
OT devices, alternative controls may be necessary and enforced at an
alternative point in the system.

proposed.text: **Govern 1.6** (AI system inventory); **Map 1.1** (operating context, since this task defines what counts as a distinct "AI entity" needing an identity).

implementations.title: Audit for and replace shared credentials, service accounts, secrets, passwords, and API keys
implementations.description:
Technically enforce distinct, cryptographically verifiable non-human
identities (NHIs - credentials designed to be issued to software/AI
agents rather than people) for every autonomous sub-agent, micro-service
hook, or transient tool invocation, particularly in AI systems built
from multiple independent parts that each act and access resources on
their own, including agentic AI systems.

Where technically feasible, prohibit the reuse of a single, shared
enterprise API key or master service account across multiple independent
agent nodes. For compute-constrained or legacy assets where unique
cryptographic identities cannot be natively generated, enforce
compensating controls at an alternative point in the system.

Relying on shared accounts or group credentials heavily degrades
situational awareness and complicates post-incident forensics because it
obscures the true root cause of an action. In a complex or chained
multi-agent system, being able to trace actions back to a unique,
non-shared programmatic identity is essential for granular attribution
and containment.

Appropriately implementing granular NHIs ensures that if an individual
model node experiences behavioral drift, runtime errors, or prompt
compromise, its specific logical tokens can be isolated and revoked by
the Security Operations Center (SOC) without invalidating the wider
multi-tiered asset application architecture.

tasks.title: Enforce principles of least agency and least privilege for AI entities
tasks.description:
Least agency requires that the system's capability to initiate
independent actions or invoke external operational tools is minimized to
only what is strictly necessary for its defined function. This is
distinct from least privilege which restricts what it is allowed to do
should access be attempted. 

This helps to ensure that systems are restricted from being granted
permanent access to control systems, configuration interfaces, or
operational tools beyond the active operational need, and that they
avoid accessing these unnecessarily even when access exists.

Require that the access permissions defined under Task 5.2: Determine and enforce specific access requirements are minimized to only
what is strictly necessary for the AI entity's defined function. 

Controls based on those applied to human users are a suitable point to
build from, with additional controls put in place to account for AI
agents and systems that may: 

-   Have limited needs and whose access should be further
    compartmentalized. 
-   Be influenced by multiple people beyond those notionally
    responsible. 
-   Interact with other AI agents and systems, resulting in potential
    emergent behavior. 
-   Operate at speeds beyond those expected of humans. 
-   May not be able to provide meaningful explanations for their
    actions.

implementations.title: Add AI disclosure to existing procurement policies
implementations.description:
Leverage existing legal/contractual workflows to provide baseline
visibility into hidden AI dependencies in standard IT/OT/ICS software,
particularly when AI features are added during otherwise routine
updates. 

Procurement policies should explicitly require AI vendors to disclose:

-   The nature and frequency of model updates, including updates that
    do not require operator action to take effect (especially 'silent'
    updates and cloud-side changes).
-   The provenance and version of training data used in each model
    release.
-   Any changes to safety-relevant model behavior introduced in each
    update.

Where feasible, establish contractual rights to suspend automatic
updates pending internal review for any AI system that influences
safety-critical CI operations. Organizations should carefully balance
this suspension mechanism against the competing risk of delaying
critical security patches or performance fixes, ensuring that any update
deferral is strictly time-bound, risk-assessed, and accompanied by
enhanced temporary monitoring.

Where such contractual obligations are unfeasible, organizations should
substitute equivalent technical compensating controls to contain update
risk. These alternative controls may include:

-   Isolated Perimeter Staging: Route all incoming software updates or
    vendor endpoint connections through isolated staging networks,
    hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) test rigs, or digital twins to execute
    initial behavioral verification before promoting the update to the
    active production path.
-   Network Egress and API Gates: Deploy strict network filtering or
    proxy blocks that restrict the AI application's ability to pull
    silent, cloud-side model changes or unvetted external dependencies
    at runtime until the connection is manually authorized by an
    administrator.
-   Temporary Safety Wrapper Tightening: Automatically adjust the
    threshold margins of the independent, deterministic safety wrappers
    (defined in Task 3.2: Implement independent guardrails ("safety wrappers") for AI...)
    during the initial post-update deployment window. This step ensures
    that any unexpected or erratic behavior introduced by the silent
    update is instantly blocked at the physical process boundary before
    it can cause operational harm.

This implementation mitigates hazard risk of a compromised AI vendor
update pipeline, where a trusted vendor's software update mechanism is
breached, delivering malicious updates to AI systems across multiple CI
operators simultaneously. 

In this scenario, the direct CI analog is an AI model that receives a
silent update changing its detection behavior, classification
thresholds, or safety logic without the operator's knowledge or review.

implementations.description:

conventional "Secure-by-Design" guidance during procurement. Require

prompting, or data schema variance. Vendors should provide clear
instructions on how the model safely degrades or transitions to backup

implementations.title: Implement Logical Policy Locks for Adaptive Models
implementations.description:
For AI systems utilizing active reinforcement learning, continuous
local fine-tuning, or dynamic prompt optimization, implement an
automated "Policy Lock" that programmatically freezes model weights
(the model's internal, learned parameters), hyper-parameters
(configuration settings that control how the model learns or operates),
and boundary logic (the programmatic code defining the safe operating
limits the system should stay within, as established in Task
3.2: Implement independent guardrails ("safety wrappers") for AI...) during active operational
windows. 

Shifting a deployed model from a static runtime state into a tuning
cycle should require a physical confirmation step or an out-of-band
administrative governance mechanism. This prevents streaming production
data or unvetted operational telemetry from silently altering the
model's learned behavioral thresholds outside of formal configuration
change control channels.

references.citation: NIST SP 800-82r3 (Section 6.2.4.2 on Configuration Change Control)

cross_references.label: 3.2: Implement independent guardrails ("safety wrappers") for AI...

proposed.text: **NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, CM-3** (Configuration Change Control). It fits treating "freezing model weights" as a formal change-control gate, consistent with the version-control framing that Task 7.3 already uses.

tasks.title: Define Authorization and Access Controls for AI Modifications
tasks.description:
Establish strict identity-based access controls for individuals
authorized to modify internal AI models, systems, AI safety mechanisms,
datasets, or configurations. 

This task implements and extends the principle of least privilege to
ensure that only qualified personnel can alter the behavior of critical
functions, reducing the risk of accidental or malicious internal
interference.

implementations.title: Define and implement requirements for approvals and logging of updates and changes to AI systems, particularly for changes to models, knowledge bases, and guardrails, especially for applications with an "automation bias" or reduced human oversight and thus where changes in behavior may not be immediately noticed.

Implement regular "integrity checks" for systems that interface with external AI services to verify that external AI systems and services have not been unexpectedly altered. This may incorporate TEVV protocols such as those from Task [2.3: Establish protocols for and regularly perform systematic, and achievable Testing, Evaluation, Validation, and Verification (TEVV)](#kix.af6uispxw0j5).

tasks.title: Conduct Impact Assessments and Risk Management for AI System and Model Updates
tasks.description:
Establish procedures for and perform structured risk and performance
assessment before deploying any internal updates to AI systems, such as
model prompts, configuration changes, data inputs, or safety wrappers.

Where increases in risk are identified, if the deployment proceeds then
mitigating controls should be identified and implemented. 

This task verifies that "minor" internal adjustments do not
unintentionally degrade overall system resilience or violate established
functional safety benchmarks and requirements (see Practice 2: Define AI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service expectations), be it through
unintentional side effects of new behaviors or "catastrophic forgetting"
(AI losing previously learned correct behavior after update or
retraining) of previous good behavior.

cross_references.label: 2: Define AI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service expectations

implementations.title: Perform pre-update validation and re-calibration before deploying any updates to models, system prompts, databases, and other components of AI systems that affect performance and safety. This should be informed by Practices [1: Establish requirements for success](#kix.c8cs921upv7k) and [2: Define AI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service expectations](#kix.za6xza2uty41).
implementations.description:
Changes to performance should be documented and, where necessary,
mitigating controls should be put in place prior to deployment. 

For example, a new model for an AI system that summarizes and
prioritizes equipment condition reports for maintenance scheduling might
have improved accuracy overall. Pre-update validation might reveal an
unacceptably higher false negative rate for specific types of equipment
that could not be addressed by re-calibrating thresholds. Mitigating
controls can then be put in place, such as having the AI system fall
back onto the previous model for reports from these types of equipment.

implementations.title: Perform automated "champion-challenger" and drift assessment by concurrently running existing production AI systems ("champion") alongside the prospective updated AI system ("challenger") in a "shadow mode" to determine the differences in behavior.
implementations.description:
The "challenger" system should demonstrate appropriate improvements in
performance, as measured in Practices 1: Establish requirements for success and 2: Define AI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service expectations, utilizing evaluation
metrics that align with Task 1.3: Implement evaluation and test plans, including TEVV,..., and mitigating controls established, prior to switch-over
to the new system. 

This process also supports Practice 9: Provide calibrated, needs-based AI risk management training in training those interacting with the system, should this be
required by any change in the behavior of the new system.
