implementations.title: Integrate Privacy Impact Assessments (PIA) into Update Cycles
implementations.description:
Conduct a PIA for all significant model or system updates to identify
risks related to data minimization, re-identification, and inference.
Ensure that updates do not bypass existing privacy controls.

references.citation: NIST Privacy Framework
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5: Personally Identifiable Information Processing and Transparency (PT-)

proposed.text: **ISO/IEC 29134:2023**, *Guidelines for privacy impact assessment*, a cross-sector standard for structuring the PIA process this implementation calls for, with the **NIST Privacy Framework 1.0** also worth citing here as NIST's companion framework to the AI RMF.

implementations.title: Audit Interoperability for Hardware or Data Substrate Substitution
implementations.description:
Establish a change-management trigger within the internal supply chain
for when physical operational components or software data feeds (e.g.,
valves, pumps, switches, or sensors, or API schemas, electronic health
record modules, or transaction journals) are replaced with equivalents
from a different vendor or manufacturer. Even if the replacement part
complies perfectly with existing engineering specifications, the
internal supply chain process should mandate a regression test of any
governing AI systems to ensure the vendor swap does not invalidate
undocumented physical dependencies embedded within the AI's learned
policy.

This implementation is highly related to Task 2.5: Verify and Ensure Policy Robustness Against Component, Hardware, and Data Schema Variance.

cross_references.label: 2.5: Verify and Ensure Policy Robustness Against Component, Hardware, and Data Schema Variance

tasks.title: Establish processes for internal AI component deprecation and decommissioning
tasks.description:
Establish secure, structured protocols for the sunsetting, deprecation,
and decommissioning of internally developed AI agents, systems, tools,
models, training datasets, and associated software dependencies. 

This task ensures that when internal AI assets reach end-of-life, they
are safely removed from production environments without breaking legacy
system dependencies or leaving behind unmonitored attack surfaces.

implementations.title: Internal Dependency Mapping (Orphan System Prevention)
implementations.description:
Before decommissioning an internal AI agent, system, tool, model or
API, mandate a comprehensive audit of the internal supply chain to
identify all downstream IT, OT, or ICS systems that rely on its outputs.
Establish strict "deprecation timelines" and notifications to ensure
dependent systems are safely refactored or reverted to deterministic
fallbacks before the model is turned off.

The process of mapping dependencies is common to Implementation
3.5.2: Identify indirect shared infrastructure and collateral damage exposure. If that mapping
has already been performed and kept current, much of the groundwork for
decommissioning will already be in place.

cross_references.label: 3.5.2: Identify indirect shared infrastructure and collateral damage exposure

implementations.title: Secure Archiving and Destruction of Model and Other AI Artifacts
implementations.description:
Define destruction (cryptographically secure as appropriate) or secure
archiving standards for retired models, training pipelines, and
datasets. This prevents "zombie models" from being accidentally used,
resurrected or exfiltrated. 

This may be particularly important for models that were found to behave
inappropriately, do not comply with regulations, are found to contain
illegal or otherwise undesirable content, or found to be susceptible to
reverse engineering and leakage of confidential or proprietary
information.

implementations.title: Legacy Logic Vulnerability Management
implementations.description:
For AI systems that cannot be immediately decommissioned due to legacy
constraints (e.g., dependent systems that cannot be updated), establish
an "Extended Isolation Protocol." This requires appropriate controls,
such as redeployment onto isolated systems, additional monitoring, or
stricter fail-over conditions, to contain risks associated with
continuing to use an otherwise deprecated system.

practices.title: Incorporate AI-aware incident analysis and response procedures
practices.description:
Develop and implement protocols for responding to and investigating
AI-related failures, addressing the unique challenges posed by
probabilistic and non-deterministic system behaviors in operational
environments. 

This practice provides the forensic clarity necessary to support
regulatory oversight, safety investigations, and situational awareness
during ongoing incident response, ensuring that AI-driven incidents do
not compromise organizational accountability or the reliable operation
of CI.

This practice focuses on governance and resourcing to satisfy
transparency and regulatory requirements. It dovetails with Practice
2: Define AI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service expectations, which focuses on
technical and functional requirements, and Practice 11: Maintain AI-aware mission continuity and disaster recovery planning, which focuses on
maintaining operations.

cross_references.label: 2: Define AI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service expectations
11: Maintain AI-aware mission continuity and disaster recovery planning

proposed.text: Root cause analysis; Digital chain of custody; Incident response; Forensics; Disclosure.

**Measure 3.1–3.3** (mechanisms for tracking, responding to, and communicating AI risks and incidents, the anchor category for this practice in this project's Practices-Index reference table); **Manage 4.1** (post-deployment monitoring), **Manage 4.3** (incidents communicated to relevant AI actors).
**Respond, Recover** (incident analysis and response is the direct CSF analog).

NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 (Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations, cited at Practice 4) as the general incident-handling anchor, extended here for AI-aware forensics; MITRE ATLAS (cited at Task 5.4) for AI-specific attack and failure taxonomy useful in root-cause classification.

tasks.title: Identify scenarios requiring deterministic root cause analysis and incident reconstruction
tasks.description:
Define the specific applications, operational thresholds, and
safety-critical triggers that mandate a comprehensive, deterministic
reconstruction of an AI-driven failure, for both post-event
investigation as well as to provide situational awareness for
immediate-term incident response. 

This task ensures that applications requiring forensic root cause
analysis are performed by AI systems that support such investigations.

It also ensures that forensic resources are prioritized for high-impact
events and that the organization meets the evidentiary standards
required for regulatory and safety oversight.

implementations.title: Evaluate AI applications
implementations.description:
Evaluate AI applications to identify the extent of root cause analysis
required to satisfy risk management and regulatory requirements. This
evaluation should explicitly screen for process paths where
deterministic forensic reconstruction is a safety or operational
requirement. Where a proposed AI system cannot satisfy these specific
analytical demands, organizations should either substitute systems
inherently capable of true root cause analysis, demonstrably close the
gap via validated compensating controls, or implement deterministic
boundaries to ensure execution hands over to manual or legacy systems
capable of the required analysis.

implementations.title: Identify AI systems that may not satisfy root cause analysis requirements
implementations.description:
Identify specific AI system classes that carry inherent forensic gaps
that cannot be fully closed by techniques like runtime telemetry. These
include large language models with non-deterministic sampling, agentic
systems with ephemeral context, and remote-hosted inference services
without preserved telemetry. In addition, some architectures and systems
rely on inherent operational randomness that may not be able to be
meaningfully replayed. 

Post-hoc explainability tools such as those based on SHAP and LIME
should not be treated as forensic proof of how or why an incident
occurred. Such techniques test a system with altered inputs and infer,
after the fact, one hypothesis for what likely drove the system's
output, without consideration for the system's actual decision making
process. 

Where such systems are identified, technical managers should
cross-reference with Task 8.2: Identify additional controls that may be required in scenarios where deterministic root cause analysis is not possible to implement mandatory
safety margins or alternative validation frameworks.

references.citation: Swidey, E. (2026). "Utilities must ask AI vendors these questions to meet critical infrastructure protection standards" Utility Dive. (Speaks directly to power utilities preparing for NERC CIP-015-1, while warning all regulated infrastructure sectors that auditors will reject post-hoc explanations as "reconstructed narratives".)

Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and International Partners (2025). "Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology." CISA. (Emphasises the need for a true "why" and "how" decisions are made.)

Haha, M. A. B., Bohli, A., Haddour, N., & Bouallegue, R. (2026). "A Systematic Review of Industrial IoT Anomaly Detection and the Forensic Interpretability Gap." MDPI Electronics. (Examining wastewater, manufacturing, and energy use cases, this review provides a global template for industrial operators by distinguishing model-centric post-hoc attributions from system-centric forensics, showing why standard correlational explainers mistake downstream symptoms for root causes.)

Slack, D., Hilgard, S., Jia, E., Singh, S., & Lakkaraju, H. (2020). "Fooling LIME and SHAP: Adversarial Attacks on Post hoc Explanation Methods." AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES). (Addressing cybersecurity threat hunters and auditors across critical networks, this study proves that perturbation-based explainers can be fooled by adversarial "scaffolding" wrappers that detect synthetic inputs and fake clean explanations during active system tampering.)

causaLens (2023). "Explainable AI (XAI) Doesn't Explain Enough." causaLens. (Details why correlational explainers fail to support high-risk operational decisions because they highlight superficial statistical associations rather than the causal dynamics of the system.)

cross_references.label: 8.2: Identify additional controls that may be required in scenarios where deterministic root cause analysis is not possible

proposed.text: **ISO/IEC 27043:2015**, *Incident investigation principles and processes*. It establishes the baseline digital-forensics assumptions (reproducibility, evidence integrity) against which this implementation's point can be framed: that certain AI system classes structurally cannot satisfy those assumptions.

implementations.title: Update existing incident response policies and playbooks to include documenting the state of AI systems at the time of the incident, such as information from Task [7.1: Maintain an Internal Registry of AI Deployments](#kix.svuun1hdnz08).

Conduct incident reconstruction drills within digital twins or high fidelity simulators to ensure that the resulting root cause analysis process and outputs are both accurate and accurately understood by responding personnel.
implementations.description:
Regular drills also detect shifts in the capabilities of underlying
systems to enable root cause analysis, particularly where AI
functionality is provided by external parties. 

This is particularly important in applications where such analysis is
required in real-time to inform ongoing, time-sensitive incident
response activities.

implementations.title: Multi-agent cascade reconstruction capabilities
implementations.description:
For deployments involving multiple cooperating or nested AI agents,
establish logging and telemetry requirements that explicitly span agent
boundaries. Telemetry should capture inter-agent communications, dynamic
delegation chains, and context window handoffs. This tracking is
necessary to trace how errors propagate through an ecosystem, ensuring
forensic investigators can accurately distinguish an originating system
anomaly from downstream algorithmic amplification.

references.citation: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic AI Applications (2025) (particularly ASI06 (Memory and Context Poisoning) to govern context integrity across chained agent handoffs).
MITRE ATLAS (utilizing the framework's multi-stage attack paths to model how localized agent failures or exploits cascade across adjacent automated systems).

proposed.text: **OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions**, a vendor-neutral technical standard for agent and LLM observability that addresses telemetry spanning agent-to-agent boundaries, which is the multi-agent traceability gap this implementation targets. This is an actively evolving standard rather than a mature one, but currently one of the few concrete technical references in the space.

tasks.title: Identify additional controls that may be required in scenarios where deterministic root cause analysis is not possible
tasks.description:
Establish formal risk-based protocols and alternative verification
standards for scenarios where the non-deterministic nature of AI
prevents a precise root-cause identification. This provides a governance
framework for making informed, defensible decisions regarding initial
system deployment and re-commissioning. 

Such systems should not be deployed in applications where forensic root
cause analysis is required by regulation or safety obligation unless
compensating controls demonstrably close the gap; otherwise,
organizations should substitute systems inherently capable of satisfying
root cause analysis requirements.

implementations.title: Identify applications and situations for which root cause analysis requirements may be relaxed with appropriate compensating risk management controls.
implementations.description:
For example, a load-balancing optimization application might typically
require forensic root-cause analysis for all actions. It may be
acceptable to revise this so that it does not require forensic
root-cause analysis for actions that differ by no more than a certain
percentage from a verified-safe (but sub-optimal) legacy system.

implementations.title: Identify opaque systems and appropriate safety margins within which they will operate to acceptably minimize the likelihood of failures for which root-cause analysis cannot be performed. These margins may be relative to other systems, as per Implementation [8.2.1: Identify applications and situations for which root cause analysis requirements may be relaxed with appropriate compensating risk management controls](#kix.ufng1i3b3l37).
implementations.description:
Beyond these safety margins, establish appropriate procedures for
hand-off to deterministic or legacy systems, or for manual oversight.

tasks.title: Designate roles for AI incident governance
tasks.description:
Formulate a cross-functional AI Incident Response Team (AIRT) that
includes representatives from legal, technical, risk management, and
communications. 

This task ensures that the high-level management of an incident is
supported by a "digital chain of command" capable of making informed
decisions regarding liability, public safety, and mission
continuity.

implementations.title: Identify internal incident management points of contact for every AI system that can affect the organization's mission, and ensure that they are resourced and well-practiced to foresee, prepare for, and manage incidents relating to their AI system(s). This includes both internally hosted AI systems and purchased-as-a-service systems.
implementations.description:
Before an incident occurs, they maintain documentation of their
system's mission-criticality, organizational impacts, fail-over options,
and dependencies. During an incident, they lead evidence-based
prioritization efforts to restore the most mission-critical functions
first, while external resources are being brought online.

implementations.title: Form a permanent AI incident governance team that includes appropriate organizational and leadership, such as the CISO, technical, and legal staff with expertise in AI, and operations management to oversee the recovery and recommissioning of AI systems following an incident.

tasks.title: Define external reporting and regulatory disclosure protocols following AI incidents
tasks.description:
Establish formal procedures and relationships with external
organizations for notifying sector-specific regulators and the public
following an AI-related anomaly. 

This task ensures that the organization meets its legal and
transparency obligations, helping to maintain community trust and
contribute to broader sector-wide threat intelligence.

implementations.title: Integrate AI-specific triggers into existing incident disclosure and reporting protocols

proposed.text: "Add AI-specific trigger conditions (for example, confirmed AI-driven safety event, unauthorized AI action, or AI system compromise) to the organization's existing incident disclosure and regulatory reporting protocols, rather than building a parallel AI-only reporting pathway. This ensures AI incidents are routed through the same accountable disclosure process as any other operational incident, with sector-specific regulators added where the existing protocol does not already cover them."

implementations.title: Establish automated notification and detailed impact disclosure for sector-specific authorities

proposed.text: "Where sector regulation requires notification within a fixed window (for example, financial-services suspicious-activity reporting deadlines, or sector-specific outage reporting), automate the trigger-to-notification pathway for confirmed AI-driven incidents so that the disclosure deadline is met without depending on manual escalation, and ensure the automated notice includes the impact detail the specific regulator requires."

tasks.title: Pre-arrange specialized resources for investigating and recovering from AI incidents
tasks.description:
Ensure that the organization has at least pre-identified, and ideally
pre-arranged, access to the specialized personnel and budgetary
resources needed for complex investigations, such as third-party AI
forensic auditors or specialized legal counsel. 

The market for third-party AI forensic auditors is currently nascent.
Interim approaches include developing internal capability through
targeted training, establishing sector-level mutual aid via ISACs and
Sector Coordinating Councils, and forming partnerships with academic
centers conducting AI security and forensics research.

This task addresses potential internal skill gaps and ensures that the
investigation of and recovery from non-deterministic AI failures is
adequately funded and supported.

implementations.title: Identify third-party AI forensic and legal experts for contingency access

proposed.text: "Pre-identify (even without a signed retainer) at least one external AI forensic specialist and one legal counsel with relevant AI incident experience, and document their contact path for activation during an incident. Where dedicated AI forensic vendors are not available or affordable, identify sector ISAC or Sector Coordinating Council mutual-aid contacts, or academic partners, as an interim substitute, consistent with the interim approaches noted in Task 8.5's description."

implementations.title: Establish formal retainer-style relationships with specialized AI incident responders and auditors

proposed.text: "Where budget allows, convert the contingency contacts identified in Implementation 8.5.1 into a formal retainer or standing services agreement, so that response time during an actual incident is not gated on new-vendor procurement. Review the retainer roster annually as the market for AI forensic services matures, per the 'currently nascent' caveat noted in this task's description."

practices.title: Provide calibrated, needs-based AI risk management training
practices.description:
Establish a systematic program for AI risk management training tailored
to specific operational roles and decision-making responsibilities.

This practice ensures that stakeholders across the organization possess
the calibrated knowledge necessary to identify AI risks and maintain
mission continuity. It also assists in preventing the safety and
security gaps that arise from over- or under-trust of automated systems.

proposed.text: Automation bias; Competency mapping; Workforce readiness; Calibrated trust.

**Govern 2.2** (AI risk management training for personnel and partners, the anchor category for this practice in this project's Practices-Index reference table); **Govern 4.1** (organizational practices to cultivate a critical-thinking, safety-first culture).
**Govern** (workforce training and role-based competency is a governance-function control in CSF terms and does not map cleanly to a technical Protect or Detect function).

NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1 and NIST SP 800-181 (NICE Workforce Framework for Cybersecurity) as the established model for role-based competency mapping, extended here to AI risk roles; the automation-bias literature cited in the parallel discussion-thread work (Parasuraman & Manzey, *Complacency and bias in human use of automation*, Human Factors 52(3), 2010) is a candidate for Task 9.2 specifically.

tasks.title: Perform role-based AI risk competency mapping
tasks.description:
Identify specific AI-related knowledge and skills required for
different organizational roles, from executive level to front-line
operations. 

This task ensures that training is targeted to the specific risks
encountered in each role and provides those responsible for mission
continuity with relevant, actionable information and practice.

implementations.title: Identify required AI literacy and risk awareness levels for existing operational roles

proposed.text: "For each existing operational role (not a new AI-specific job title), determine the minimum AI literacy and risk-awareness level needed to safely perform that role's current responsibilities, ranging from basic awareness for occasional AI-output consumers to deep technical competency for those configuring or overriding AI systems. Use this to right-size training investment rather than applying uniform training across all roles."

implementations.title: Develop a comprehensive AI risk competency matrix and personalized learning paths

proposed.text: "Consolidate the per-role requirements from Implementation 9.1.1 into a single competency matrix mapping roles to required competencies and current gaps, and use it to assign individualized training paths rather than a one-size-fits-all curriculum. Revisit the matrix whenever a role's exposure to AI systems changes materially."

tasks.title: Deliver specialized training on human-AI interaction and automation bias
tasks.description:
Provide operational personnel with the skills to recognize and mitigate
"automation bias", the tendency to over-trust automated outputs, and
other psychological factors that lead to miscalibrated over or under
trust. 

This task reduces the risk of human error during AI-driven anomalies
and ensures that manual overrides remain an effective and timely
safety-net for critical infrastructure functions.

implementations.title: Include role-specific training on "AI failure modes" in standard annual technical or cybersecurity training
implementations.description:
This training should include identifying applications and situations in
which personnel in that role may use, interact with, or supervise AI
systems; the potential mission impact of AI system failures; situations
in which AI systems should be overridden; the procedure for safely doing
so; how to obtain the necessary situational awareness; and
communication, reporting, and documentation requirements. 

This implementation mitigates hazard risk of an operator accepting an
incorrect AI recommendation without independent verification, because
repeated correct outputs have conditioned them to treat AI
recommendations as authoritative. This is an emerging human factors
failure mode specific to AI-driven automation and assistants, and as
such is not yet well addressed by traditional security frameworks and
guidance. It applies wherever personnel supervise, interact with, or can
override AI systems in CI operational environments. 

Because established frameworks offer limited pre-built guidance,
organizations should proactively extend existing TEVV protocols (Task
1.3: Implement evaluation and test plans, including TEVV,...) to probe for this
specific failure mode, use qualified engineering and operational
judgment to anticipate how automation bias might manifest in their
particular application before an incident forces the question, and
incorporate the results into ongoing training.

It provides a structural template for the role-specific curriculum this implementation calls for, complementing the automation-bias literature (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010) already suggested for this practice's References field in the companion TBD-Suggestions document.

implementations.title: Implement realistic incident simulation training for personnel who play a significant AI risk management role, such as those supervising or expected to take over from AI systems. This may include the use of digital twins and realistic simulation environments, both to generate test scenarios and to determine the kinds of failures that are realistic.
implementations.description:
Particular care should be taken in situations where the existence or
nature of an AI system failure or error may be hidden or non-obvious,
particularly due to other errors in related AI systems. 

For example, hallucinations in an AI-based summarization or dashboard
system may result in early reports of failure from upstream systems
being downplayed, omitted, or presented in a confusing or misleading
manner, particularly where those reports are very unusual.

tasks.title: Establish audit-ready systems for verifying workforce readiness
tasks.description:
Create formal mechanisms to assess and document the effectiveness of AI
risk training through structured assessments, tabletop simulations, and
periodic drills. 

This task provides the verifiable evidence of "Workforce Readiness"
required for regulatory compliance and ensures that personnel maintain
the calibrated judgment necessary for high-stakes decision-making across
the AI lifecycle.

implementations.title: Maintain logs of completed AI training and basic proficiency assessment scores

proposed.text: "Record completion of required AI risk training and any associated proficiency assessment scores per individual, tied to the role-based requirements from Task 9.1, in a form that can be produced on demand for regulatory or internal audit review. This is the minimum audit-ready evidence layer beneath the readiness drills in Implementation 9.3.2."

implementations.title: Implement periodic "readiness drills" and validated skills certifications for critical roles

proposed.text: "For roles identified as critical under Implementation 9.1.1 (for example, those authorized to override AI systems under Practice 4), require periodic hands-on readiness drills or simulations in addition to training completion, with a validated certification renewal cadence. This closes the gap between completed training and demonstrated capability under pressure."

practices.title: Implement multi-tiered AI system logging and audit capabilities
practices.description:
Establish a framework for the systematic capture and preservation of
operational telemetry across the AI lifecycle to ensure decision-making
logic remains transparent and verifiable. 

This practice supports the development of audit-ready systems that
support forensic investigations and regulatory compliance, providing the
foundational data required to maintain organizational accountability for
automated actions in critical infrastructure.

references.citation: OMB M-26-14 Ensuring Effective and Efficient Agency Logging and Network Visibility to Defend Against Evolving Cyber Threats

proposed.text: Telemetry; Audit trail; Traceability; Chain of custody; Tamper-evidence.

**Measure 2.8** (transparency and accountability, the anchor category for this practice in this project's Practices-Index reference table); **Govern 1.4–1.5** (documentation and reporting mechanisms); **Manage 4.1** (post-deployment monitoring).
**Detect, Identify** (logging and audit is the evidentiary backbone for detection and for maintaining an accurate operational picture).

tasks.description:
Specify the AI systems and applications for which information,
including system inputs, outputs, system prompts, and version-specific
metadata, will be captured to ensure automated actions are
deterministically reconstructable or statistically reproducible, and

organization possesses the necessary runtime context to perform the

metrics of Practice 1: Establish requirements for success, and verify the
quality-of-service bounds of Practice 2: Define AI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service expectations.

implementations.title: Identify AI systems that may take or directly influence mission-critical actions
implementations.description:
Ensure that they are appropriately inventoried (Implementation
7.1.1: Create and maintain a "Master AI Asset List") and that logs of inputs,
outputs, and other data to reconstruct their decisions are stored in
accordance with data retention and regulatory requirements. 

Where this information is already logged (e.g., by other OT/ICS
systems) ensure that appropriate metadata is also logged and retention
policies synchronized to ensure that this information can be merged
after-the-fact.

cross_references.label: 7.1.1: Create and maintain a "Master AI Asset List"

implementations.title: Immutable Runtime Telemetry and Artifact Tracking
implementations.description:
Mandate the capture of immutable runtime telemetry at an appropriate
level of abstraction. For generated execution artifacts (such as code,
Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) logic, configurations, or automated
procedures), logs should uniquely link the output to the specific model
version and prompt context. Statistical approximations generated after
the fact by post-hoc evaluation tools (such as LIME or SHAP) should not
be relied on as a substitute for true decision-level logs. See
Implementation 8.1.2: Identify AI systems that may not satisfy... for further
details.

cross_references.label: 8.1.2: Identify AI systems that may not satisfy...

implementations.title: Forensic Integrity and Privacy-Preserving Log Partitioning
implementations.description:
Incorporate automated data-masking, encryption, and sanitization
boundaries to ensure log collection does not inadvertently retain
protected privacy data within open, day-to-day operational repositories.
Where a structural conflict exists, organizations should explicitly
define which data fields are essential to root-cause reconstruction
(Practice 8: Incorporate AI-aware incident analysis and response procedures) and restrict masking
only to non-essential elements to preserve actionable incident utility.
For high-consequence applications processing sensitive person-centric
data, such as healthcare clinical support decisions or financial
transaction journals, the "immutable" tracking mandate of Task
10.2: Establish data integrity and tamper-evidence controls... should be achieved by
routing the raw, unredacted text and prompt history (the exact model
inputs and outputs) directly into highly secured, tamper-evident storage
environments that are logically separated from routine operational
visibility. This ensures strict compliance with data privacy boundaries
without compromising the availability or validity of the audit
trail.

cross_references.label: 8: Incorporate AI-aware incident analysis and response procedures
10.2: Establish data integrity and tamper-evidence controls...

implementations.title: Asynchronous Token Logging for Constrained Edges
implementations.description:
For bandwidth-constrained, remote, or legacy edge environments where
continuous, high-volume raw transfer is unfeasible, satisfy the
immutable tracking mandate via edge-side log compression or secure local
storage paired with delayed, off-peak batch telemetry transfers to the
central log management infrastructure, or high-level metadata
reviews.

tasks.title: Establish data integrity and tamper-evidence controls for AI telemetry and logging
tasks.description:
Implement appropriate access controls and security protocols to ensure
the immutability and reliability of captured AI system logs. 

This task protects the "digital chain of custody," preventing
unauthorized modification of operational records and ensuring that audit
data remains a trustworthy source of truth for regulatory oversight and
liability management.

implementations.title: Ensure that logs are stored in an immutable manner
implementations.description:
If existing logging facilities are being used, ensure that they can
handle the potential additional bandwidth and storage capacity
requirements of AI systems without interfering with other logging
activities. 

For example, it is necessary to ensure that AI logging bandwidth does
not "flood out" logging from other devices, such as edge devices, and
that the additional storage requirements do not result in logs being
deleted earlier than is required. 

See Implementation [10.1.4: Asynchronous Token Logging for
Constrained Edges](#id.vdwbfkx1mlpw) for
bandwidth-constrained, remote, or legacy edge environments where this is
not feasible.

tasks.title: Implement systematic audit review and performance trend analysis
tasks.description:
Define formal procedures for the periodic review of AI system logs to
identify model drift, emerging biases, or performance anomalies. 

This task transforms raw telemetry into actionable oversight, allowing
technical management to detect degrading model reliability or "silent"
failures before they escalate into mission-critical incidents or cause
quality of service issues.

implementations.title: Conduct periodic manual reviews of AI logs for performance issues or drift

proposed.text: "Establish a defined cadence (for example, weekly or monthly, scaled to system criticality) for a qualified reviewer to manually examine AI system logs for signs of performance degradation, drift, or emerging bias not already caught by automated monitoring. Document findings and route any confirmed issues into the anomaly-handling process defined under Task 3.4."

implementations.title: Implement automated trend analysis and dashboarding for continuous audit oversight

proposed.text: "Build automated trend analysis and dashboards over the log data captured under Task 10.1 so that drift and anomaly signals are visible continuously rather than only at the manual-review cadence set in Implementation 10.3.1. Automated dashboards should flag threshold breaches for the manual reviewer rather than replace human judgment on borderline cases."

practices.title: Maintain AI-aware mission continuity and disaster recovery planning
practices.description:
Establish a strategic framework for mission continuity to manage the
immediate term alternative operating modes, and the longer-term recovery
and restoration of essential functions following a significant AI
failure. 

This practice highlights the need to pre-allocate recovery resources
and deliberately prioritize service restoration to ensure organizational
resilience.

This practice focuses on the "Plan B" when an incident occurs. It
dovetails with Practice 4: Define procedures for emergency avoidance override, recovery, and situation awareness, which focuses on
technical aspects that support this practice, and Practice 8: Incorporate AI-aware incident analysis and response procedures, which focuses on
governance obligations.

cross_references.label: 4: Define procedures for emergency avoidance override, recovery, and situation awareness
8: Incorporate AI-aware incident analysis and response procedures

proposed.text: Business continuity; Disaster recovery; Graceful degradation; Fail-to-manual; Restoration priority.

**Manage 2.4** (mechanisms in place to supersede, disengage, or deactivate AI systems that demonstrate unreliable behavior, the anchor category for this practice in this project's Practices-Index reference table); **Manage 4.1, 4.3** (monitoring and incident communication); **Govern 1.7** (processes for decommissioning or disengaging AI systems safely).

**Recover** (this practice's core subject, restoring essential functions after an AI-driven disruption, is the direct CSF Recover function; Respond may also apply where continuity planning overlaps with active incident handling).

NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 (Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems) as the general continuity-planning anchor; ISO 22301:2019 (Business Continuity Management Systems) as the cross-sector standard already flagged as relevant to this practice elsewhere in this reviewer community's crosswalk work; NIST SP 800-82r3 §6.2.4.5 (cited at Task 11.2) for OT-specific graceful-degradation guidance.

tasks.title: Identify and prioritize AI-dependent essential functions
tasks.description:
Catalog all infrastructure services that rely on AI components and rank
them based on their impact on mission continuity and public safety.

This task ensures that "Restoration Priorities" are established as a
matter of policy, directing limited recovery resources toward the most
critical life-safety and service-delivery functions first. It also
prioritizes the allocation of resources to maintain non-AI backup
systems for critical functions.

implementations.title: Rank operational processes based on the impact of AI failure or unavailability

proposed.text: "Rank the organization's operational processes by the severity of impact if their supporting AI component became unavailable or failed, using the same impact criteria the organization already applies to non-AI business-continuity planning where possible, rather than building a separate AI-specific criticality scale. This ranking drives the resource pre-allocation decisions in Task 11.3."

implementations.title: Conduct comprehensive AI dependency mapping across all sector-critical functions

proposed.text: "Extend the ranking in Implementation 11.1.1 into a full dependency map showing which sector-critical functions rely, directly or indirectly, on which AI components, including cases where an AI dependency is embedded several layers deep in a vendor's own stack. This map is what prevents hidden AI dependencies from being missed during continuity planning."

tasks.title: Define manual and alternative operating procedures for long-term mission continuity
tasks.description:
Develop and document comprehensive "Manual Mode" instructions for
running essential functions for extended periods without AI support.
These playbooks should define orchestrated fallback pathways tailored to
the system's operational timeline:

-   For critical systems requiring 24/7 availability, they should
    dictate the process for a safe transition to a legacy deterministic
    systems without interrupting availability.
-   For critical systems that do not need to be realtime (such as
    financial fraud queues, non-emergency triage systems, or
    administrative compliance tools), they should outline the protocols
    to safely pull the AI infrastructure offline while minimizing other
    risks, such as security and data corruption, and route accumulated
    tasks into structured manual workflows. 

This task complements those of Practice 4: Define procedures for emergency avoidance override, recovery, and situation awareness by providing the
operational playbook for sustained, non-automated service delivery
during a prolonged outage.

references.citation: NIST SP 800-82r3 (Section 6.2.4.5 on Response and Recovery Plans, featuring "graceful degradation" and the need to safely accumulate backlogs)

cross_references.label: 4: Define procedures for emergency avoidance override, recovery, and situation awareness

proposed.text: **NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1**, *Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems*, the general continuity-planning anchor already suggested at the Practice 11 level in the companion TBD-Suggestions document and reinforced here at the task level. **ISO 22301:2019** (Business Continuity Management Systems) is a cross-sector structural template for the "Manual Mode" playbooks this task calls for.

implementations.title: Document basic manual fallback procedures for AI-dependent control points

proposed.text: "For each AI-dependent control point identified in Implementation 11.1.1 and 11.1.2, document the minimum manual procedure needed to keep the function operating, even at reduced efficiency, without the AI component. This is the entry-level continuity artifact that Implementation 11.2.2's validated Safe Operating Mode builds on for the highest-criticality functions."

implementations.title: Develop a validated "Safe Operating Mode" that runs independently of AI infrastructure

proposed.text: "For the highest-criticality functions identified in Task 11.1, develop and formally validate a Safe Operating Mode: a complete, tested operating procedure that runs entirely independently of AI infrastructure, rather than relying on the informal fallback documented in Implementation 11.2.1. Validation should include the periodic drills required under Task 11.5."

tasks.title: Pre-allocate operational resources for alternative service delivery
tasks.description:
Ensure the availability and maintenance of physical tools, trained
standby personnel, and budgetary reserves required to perform fail-over
to non-AI backup systems, which may be less efficient and require
additional resources and oversight. 

While Task 8.5: Pre-arrange specialized resources for investigating and recovering from AI incidents secures investigation
experts, this task secures the operational resources needed to keep the
water flowing or the power on while the AI is offline.

cross_references.label: 8.5: Pre-arrange specialized resources for investigating and recovering from AI incidents

implementations.title: Identify standby personnel and physical tools required for manual operations

proposed.text: "Identify and document the specific personnel (by role, with backup coverage) and physical tools or equipment required to execute the manual fallback and Safe Operating Mode procedures from Task 11.2, and confirm their availability on the same cadence as other continuity resources. This is distinct from Task 8.5's forensic and investigative resourcing: this task secures the resources to keep the function running, not to investigate why it failed."

implementations.title: Maintain Isolated Standby Infrastructure and Allocated Reserves

proposed.text: "Maintain standby infrastructure (for example, non-AI backup control systems, isolated network segments, or reserve capacity) in a state ready for activation, and periodically verify, not just assume, that it remains functional and isolated from the primary AI-dependent infrastructure it is meant to replace."

tasks.title: Establish system integrity re-validation and re-commissioning protocols
tasks.description:
Define the mandatory technical benchmarks and safety tests a system
should pass before it is allowed to transition from manual mode back to
automated operations. Re-validation testing pathways should explicitly
reference and execute the TEVV protocols established in Task
1.3: Implement evaluation and test plans, including TEVV,.... 

This ensures that "turning the AI back on" does not introduce new
cascading risks and is supported by verifiable, auditable evidence of
system health.

cross_references.label: 1.3: Implement evaluation and test plans, including TEVV,...

implementations.title: Define a checklist for validating system safety before re-engaging AI control

proposed.text: "Define a mandatory pre-re-engagement checklist, referencing the TEVV protocols established in Task 1.3, that must be completed and signed off before an AI system is returned to active control after an outage or manual-mode period. The checklist should verify both technical health and that no undetected configuration drift occurred while the system was offline."

implementations.title: Implement "Shadow Mode" validation and mandatory safety-interlock checks for AI re-commissioning

proposed.text: "Before fully returning control to the AI system, run it in shadow mode, receiving live inputs and producing recommendations without executing them, alongside the active manual or fallback control, and compare outputs for a defined validation period. Require mandatory safety-interlock checks to pass before shadow mode is allowed to transition to active control."

tasks.title: Execute periodic mission continuity simulations and stress tests
tasks.description:
Conduct regular "fail-to-manual" exercises to verify that alternative
operating procedures are effective and that personnel are capable of
maintaining the mission under stress. 

This provides the audit-ready evidence of organizational preparedness
required for regulatory oversight and identifies gaps in the continuity
framework.

These exercises should be performed both during development, to ensure
that resilience is "baked in," and when in operation, to ensure that
resilience is maintained despite changes in the operating environment,
task, and condition of the system.

implementations.title: Conduct annual "fail-to-manual" tabletop exercises for key personnel

proposed.text: "Conduct at least annual tabletop exercises walking key personnel through a simulated AI failure and the transition to manual fallback procedures from Task 11.2, without requiring actual system disruption. Use findings to update the manual procedures and the personnel and resource pre-allocation from Task 11.3."

implementations.title: Execute high-fidelity simulation drills involving total AI infrastructure loss and recovery
implementations.description:
Exercises should periodically include a scenario in which the
underlying cause is not immediately apparent, to test whether personnel
can maintain continuity while the nature of the failure, accidental or
deliberate, is still being determined.

proposed.text: "For the highest-criticality functions, supplement tabletop exercises with high-fidelity simulation drills that exercise a full AI infrastructure loss and the complete recovery sequence through Task 11.4's re-commissioning checklist, at a cadence proportionate to the function's criticality tier. These drills provide the strongest evidence of organizational preparedness and should surface gaps tabletop exercises alone would miss."

practices.title: Validate AI-Generated Operational Logic and Artifacts
practices.description:
Establish rigorous validation and verification protocols for
AI-generated artifacts, including code, configurations, and procedures,
that direct or influence the execution of critical infrastructure
operations. 

This practice ensures that machine-authored code, configurations, and
procedures are scrutinized against formal specifications and tacit
institutional knowledge, preventing the deployment of 'plausible but
inaccurate' logic in high-consequence IT, OT, and ICS
environments.

proposed.text: Plausible hallucination; Formal specification; Code review; Machine-authored artifacts; Rollback.

**Measure 2.1** (test sets), **Measure 2.3** (performance), **Measure 2.5** (validity and reliability), **Measure 2.9** (explainability); **Map 3.1** (AI capabilities and limitations relative to context); **Manage 1.1** (achievement of intended purpose). This matches the mapping already established in this project's Practices-Index reference table.
**Protect** (validation and verification of machine-authored artifacts before they can act on infrastructure is a preventive control, closest to CSF Protect).

NIST AI 600-1 (cited at Task 12.2) as the general anchor; ANSI/CTA-2135 or ISO/IEC 42001 Annex A.6 (both identified as candidate crosswalks for this practice in this project's reference-index work) for formal validation-process standards applicable to AI-generated code and configuration review.

tasks.title: Establish Governance and Accountability for AI-Generated Execution Artifacts
tasks.description:
Define the policy framework and responsibility structures for the
creation, classification, and authorization of AI-generated logic. This
task ensures that every machine-authored artifact---from code to
procedural summaries---is assigned a risk tier and a clear human owner
responsible for its final approval and operational deployment.

implementations.title: Artifact Risk Classification
implementations.description:
Categorize AI-generated logic and outputs (artifacts) based on their
potential for harm if incorrect, using both proximity to execution and
influence on human decisions as evaluative criteria. To ensure
appropriate validation velocity, organizations should explicitly
distinguish between 'Direct-Execution Logic' (which directly commands
physical or digital assets like Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) code
or system configurations, requiring automated validation gates) and
'Human-Mediated Logic' (which influences human choices like procedural
summaries or diagnostic reports, relying on structured expert review
workflows).

Artifacts such as PLC code, Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition
(SCADA) configurations or automated control parameters may carry the
highest execution risk as they have close proximity to execution. 

For example:

-   AI-generated valve control logic is likely to be classified as a
    High Risk, Direct Execution artifact. 
-   Artifacts such as procedure summaries, condition reports or
    operational recommendations carry risk in proportion to the
    consequence of human actions they may influence. 

-   AI-generated summary of a maintenance procedure should be
    classified as High Risk Human Mediated artifacts due to safety
    consequences if incorrect.
-   A draft internal email summary of this same procedure that is
    subject to ongoing human brainstorming and refinement might be
    classified as Low Risk.

implementations.title: Provenance and Traceability
implementations.description:
(Referencing Task 10.1: Define decision-level logging and metadata retention policies)
Establish metadata requirements that uniquely link any generated code or
procedure to the specific model version, prompt, and "inference
context" used to create it. Validation leads should rely strictly on
this hard configuration data for audit paths, rather than relying on
post-hoc explanation tools which can mistake downstream symptoms for the
root cause of an artifact error. See Implementation 8.1.2: Identify AI systems that may not satisfy... for further details.

cross_references.label: 10.1: Define decision-level logging and metadata retention policies
8.1.2: Identify AI systems that may not satisfy...

implementations.title: Authorization of Machine-Authored Logic
implementations.description:
Define which roles (e.g., Lead Engineer, Site Supervisor) are
authorized to "promote" AI-generated logic from a draft state to a
production-ready operational artifact.

tasks.title: Implement Multi-Layered Validation of Machine-Authored Logic
tasks.description:
Deploy a hybrid verification strategy that subjects AI-generated
outputs to both deterministic automated testing and expert human
scrutiny. By checking artifacts against formal specifications and tacit
domain knowledge, this task ensures that machine-generated instructions
remain within safe operational boundaries and are free from 'plausible
hallucinations'.

references.citation: NIST AI 600-1 (guiding validation frameworks to address safety, accuracy, and hidden tech-debt risks inherent to generative AI-authored logic and code).

proposed.text: **IEEE 7001-2021**, *Transparency of Autonomous Systems*, which provides criteria for validating machine-authored logic against explainability and tacit-knowledge scrutiny, complementing NIST AI 600-1's safety and accuracy focus with a transparency lens. **ISO/IEC 42001:2023 Annex A.6** (flagged elsewhere in this project's reference-index work as a candidate crosswalk for this practice) also fits the management-system-level validation controls this task describes.

implementations.title: Deterministic and Rule-Based Guardrails
implementations.description:
(Referencing Task 3.2: Implement independent guardrails ("safety wrappers") for AI outputs)
Mandate that all AI-generated executable artifacts (like network
configurations or PLC logic) pass through non-AI, deterministic
verifiers---such as static code analyzers or schema validators---to
ensure they meet hard-coded safety constraints.

cross_references.label: 3.2: Implement independent guardrails ("safety wrappers") for AI outputs

implementations.title: Subject Matter Expert (SME) Review of Procedures
implementations.description:
For non-executable but safety-critical artifacts (like procedural
summaries), require a "red-team" review by SMEs to ensure no
"plausible hallucinations" have introduced safety risks or omitted
critical warnings (as discussed in Implementation 2.4.3: Technical Accuracy and "Plausible Hallucination" Audits).

cross_references.label: 2.4.3: Technical Accuracy and "Plausible Hallucination" Audits

implementations.title: Validation against Tacit and Formal Requirements
implementations.description:
(Referencing Task 1.4.4: Requirements for AI-Generated Code, Configurations, Procedures, and Other Logic) Ensure the validation
process explicitly checks the generated logic against both codified
technical standards and the "unwritten" operational norms of the
specific facility.

cross_references.label: 1.4.4: Requirements for AI-Generated Code, Configurations, Procedures, and Other Logic

tasks.title: Manage Operational Continuity and Resilience for Generated Artifacts
tasks.description:
Establish safeguards to protect system availability and safety
throughout the lifecycle of AI-generated logic. This includes utilizing
isolated testing environments, maintaining strict version control for
machine-authored artifacts, and ensuring the immediate availability of
human-verified 'known-good' configurations for rapid rollback and
recovery.

implementations.title: Isolated Execution Testing (Sandboxing)
implementations.description:
Where feasible, test AI-generated configurations or code in a digital
twin or isolated simulation environment before deployment to production
systems.

implementations.title: Version Control and Rollback Procedures
implementations.description:
Maintain a strict version history of all AI-generated operational
logic. Ensure that a "known-good" human-verified configuration or
procedure is always available as a fallback in the event of an
AI-generated logic failure.

implementations.title: Monitoring for Latent Failures
implementations.description:
Establish monitoring for systems running on AI-generated configurations
to detect "drift" or latent errors that may not be apparent during the
initial validation phase.
